newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Occidental sets force majeure in Cano Limon field.
newsitem.headline: Occidental sets force majeure in Cano Limon field.

text.p: Occidental Petroleum Corp declared force majeure in its 180,000 barrel per day Cano Limon oil field in eastern Colombia Tuesday after a spate of leftist rebel attacks on a major pipeline, a company spokesman said.

The attacks on the pipeline, which runs from Cano Limon in Arauca province to the Caribbean coast lifting terminal at Covenas, forced Occidental to shut in its field last Thursday after it was left without sufficient capacity to store crude on site.

"We're declaring force majeure in Cano Limon in the face of the uncertainty over how long this situation could last and in consideration of our contractual obligations," an Occidental spokesman told Reuters.
He said the declaration meant a number of contracts would be suspended and that as many as 200 contract workers and direct employees would be temporarily laid off while the emergency lasted.
The spokesman said some workers would be kept on site to carry out "indispensable" maintenance work and repairs of electricity generating plants.

The spokesman was unable to give an estimate of the cost of suspending production and of declaring force majeure, saying: "It's premature to quantify the cost of this situation. We're in the process of trying to estimate it."
He added that it was possible that some of the 135 wells in the Cano Limon field could be damaged by the shut-in.
"The possibility exists that some of the wells could be damaged. It's a technical issue and we hope the effects can be minimized," the spokesman said.
Occidental operates the field in association with state-run oil company Ecopetrol and the Royal Dutch Shell Group.

Ecopetrol, declared force majeure on some crude shipments Monday but the Occidental spokesman was not immediately able to say whether any of Occidental's or Shell's delivery commitments would be affected.

The emergency affecting the Cano Limon field and the Cano Limon-Covenas pipeline, which has a 300,000 barrel per day capacity, is the worst attack on Colombia's oil infrastructure in almost a decade since leftist guerrillas dynamited the Covenas lifting terminal, an Ecopetrol spokesman said.
The pipeline has been out of operation since July 6 when it was blown up by National Liberation Army (ELN) rebels near the town of Arauquita in Arauca province.
The line briefly began pumping crude again on July 10 after emergency repairs but was dynamited for a second time just one hour later -- forcing Occidental to shut in the Cano Limon field.
Ecopetrol repair teams from the state-run oil company Ecopetrol have been unable to get near the blast site because of continued rebel activity in the area.

An Ecopetrol spokesman said Tuesday the pipeline had been attacked a third time near the town of Cucuta, in northeast Norte de Santander province. It was not immediately clear whether the attack had been carried in the early hours Tuesday or whether it was the result of a previously undiscovered attack.

The Cano Limon pipeline has now been attacked 38 times this year compared with 47 times in 1996. Since it came into operation in 1986 it has been blasted at least 474 times, according to Ecopetrol, and more than 1.5 million barrels of crude have been spilled.
The Cuban-inspired ELN, set up by radical Roman Catholic priests in 1966, specializes in attacks on the country's key oil infrastructure.
